sections.section_title: The Greater Obligation Arising from the Greater Revelation
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage constructs a qal wahomer (lesser to greater) argument: if violations of the Torah, given through angels, received just penalties, then neglecting the salvation spoken through the Son -- who is greater than angels -- carries even graver consequences.
sections.relevance: The passage directly addresses the consequence of a believer's failure to attend to the salvation received. The rhetorical question 'how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?' expects the answer: we will not escape. The danger described is not active apostasy but passive drift (pararrheō, a nautical term for slipping past a harbor) and careless neglect (ameleō). The author includes himself in the warning ('we'), indicating this applies to those already within the community of faith. The logic is inescapable within the author's own argument: greater revelation entails greater accountability, and inattention to the Son's message produces inescapable consequences.
key_phrases: how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation
every transgression and disobedience received a just reward

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this section uses Psalm 8 to describe humanity's intended vocation -- dominion, glory, and honor over creation -- and notes that this vocation has not been put under the subjection of angels but remains assigned to humanity.

sections.section_title: The Observation That Breaks Open the Psalm
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies this half-verse as the author's observation that Psalm 8's promise of total dominion remains empirically unfulfilled: 'we do not yet see all things put under him,' establishing a gap between promise and present reality.

sections.section_title: The Pivot -- But We See Jesus
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this verse applies Psalm 8's language to Jesus: he was made lower than the angels temporarily, tasted death for everyone by the grace of God, and was crowned with glory and honor -- fulfilling in one person what the psalm promised for humanity.

sections.section_title: The Pioneer Made Complete Through Suffering
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this verse describes God's decision to bring many sons to glory by making the pioneer of their salvation perfect through sufferings -- the perfecting is experiential consecration for the role, not correction of a moral defect.

sections.section_title: Shared Origin, Shared Identity -- Three Scriptural Proofs
sections.summary: The neutral reading shows the author establishes the kinship between Jesus and believers through their common origin, supported by three scriptural citations (Psalm 22:22, Isaiah 8:17, Isaiah 8:18) that portray Jesus as declaring God's name among his brethren and standing with his children as a faithful remnant.

sections.section_title: The Incarnation, Death, and the Defeat of the Devil
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this section explains why the Son shared in flesh and blood: to destroy through death the one who held the power of death (the devil) and to free those enslaved by lifelong fear of death, taking hold of Abraham's seed rather than angels.

sections.section_title: The Result -- A Merciful and Faithful High Priest
sections.summary: The neutral reading identifies this as the first introduction of Jesus as 'High Priest' in the letter, grounded in his full identification with humanity, qualified to make propitiation for the sins of the people and able to aid those who are tempted because he himself suffered while being tempted.
